posts.title: You drove home drunk this morning
posts.why_shared: Shock hook night workers screenshot and send to the coworker who drives home after doubles.
posts.caption: You'd never drive after drinks. But after a night shift? In one study, 24 hours awake impaired performance about as much as a 0.10% blood alcohol level (Dawson & Reid, Nature, 1997). What's your longest shift? #nightshift #drowsydriving #nurselife #emtlife #sleepscience

slides.text: You drove home drunk this morning.

slides.label: 17 hours awake
slides.title: Your brain hits ~0.05%
slides.body: That's what one study found: performance like a 0.05% blood alcohol level.

slides.label: 24 hours awake
slides.title: Now it's ~0.10%
slides.body: Over the legal driving limit in every US state. And here's the part that gets you...

slides.label: Do the math
slides.title: Up at 8am. Off at 7am.
slides.body: First night of the week? That's 23 hours awake before you even start the car.

slides.label: The scary part
slides.title: It doesn't feel that bad
slides.body: Willpower and experience don't cancel it out. Coffee in the parking lot isn't a fix either.

slides.label: Save this
slides.title: Before you drive home
slides.body: Nap 15-20 min first, carpool after long stretches, or get a ride. Nodding off? Pull over.

posts.title: The 20 minutes that ruin your day sleep
posts.why_shared: Names a mistake every night worker makes daily; high save value for the drive-home tip.
posts.caption: Can't fall asleep after a night shift? Your commute home might be why. Morning light is your body clock's strongest wake-up signal. In one study, dark sunglasses on the way home helped night workers adapt (Crowley et al., 2003). Only wear very dark lenses if someone else is driving. #nightshift #nightshiftnurse #sleeptips #circadianrhythm #shiftwork

slides.text: The 20 minutes that ruin your day sleep
slides.sub: It happens before you get home

slides.label: It's not your bed
slides.title: It's your drive home
slides.body: Clock out at 7am and walk straight into sunrise. That's the problem.

slides.label: Here's why
slides.title: Morning light = 'wake up'
slides.body: Bright morning light is the strongest signal your body clock gets to start the day.

slides.label: So your brain thinks...
slides.title: 'Great, it's daytime'
slides.body: Right when you need to sleep. Exhausted, but staring at the ceiling at 9am? This is you.

slides.label: The research
slides.title: Dark lenses on the way home
slides.body: Night workers who blocked morning light on the commute adapted far better to night shifts.
slides.source: Source: Crowley et al., J Biol Rhythms, 2003

slides.label: Save this
slides.title: How to block it safely
slides.body: Riding home? Dark wraparound sunglasses. Driving? Only normal driving sunglasses. Skip errands, go straight to a dark room.

posts.title: Your 8 hours of day sleep isn't 8 hours
posts.why_shared: Challenges a belief night workers hold; the 'how many do you really get' question floods comments.
posts.caption: Time in bed isn't time asleep. More than half of night-shift workers report 6 hours of sleep or less (CDC NIOSH), partly because your body clock fights day sleep. How many hours do you actually get after a night shift? #nightshift #shiftwork #sleepscience #nurselife #sleepbetter

slides.text: Your 8 hours of day sleep isn't 8 hours

slides.label: The reality
slides.title: Over half get 6 hours or less
slides.body: That's night-shift workers in CDC NIOSH training data. But why, if you're in bed long enough?
slides.source: Source: CDC NIOSH, shift work training

slides.label: The reason
slides.title: Your body clock fights back
slides.body: It pushes you awake late morning, no matter how tired you are.

slides.label: Then add...
slides.title: Daylight. Traffic. Texts.
slides.body: Every wake-up you don't remember still cuts your real sleep. In bed 8, asleep maybe 5.

slides.label: Most people miss this
slides.title: It stacks up all week
slides.body: A short night after every shift adds up. That's the 'tired on my day off' feeling.

slides.label: Save this
slides.title: Protect your day sleep
slides.body: Full blackout. Earplugs or white noise. Phone on Do Not Disturb. Same sleep window every work day.

slides.text: Be honest: how many hours do you really get?
